ethics_check.report:

> We specifically examined RA manifestations in primary school children and early-and-mid adolescents who were enrolled in two respective studies designed to oversample participants with RD.

> Participants were included in the current study if they completed the RA questionnaire and correctly responded to an embedded attention-check item (i.e., "Please select 'sometimes' for this question."), ensuring data quality and adherence to task instructions.

> In both datasets, parents reported that participants had normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision; no parents reported autism, intellectual disability or other serious neurodevelopmental conditions.

> Adolescent participants were recruited virtually from across the United States and included both typically developing readers and individuals with specific learning disabilities.

table.header: No Significant Gender Differences in RA within Children and Adolescent Groups

table.text: Although the present findings did not provide evidence of age-or gender-related differences nor differences across different quantiles, smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Post hoc sensitivity power analyses indicated that our samples had reasonable sensitivity to detect effects of small to moderate magnitudes or larger but limited sensitivity to smaller effects. Furthermore, the 95% confidence intervals for the nonsignificant results included both negative and positive values, showing relatively wide range, indicating uncertainty regarding the magnitude and direction of potential differences. Future studies with larger samples are needed to improve sensitivity to smaller effects and obtain more precise estimates of age-and genderrelated differences in RA, as well as potential variation in RA-reading associations across the distribution of reading performance.
table.header: Limitations and Future Directions

table.text: To provide an indirect benchmark for the statistical sensitivity of the quantile regression analyses, we conducted OLS-based power sensitivity analyses with age included as a covariate (pwr package in R, Champely, 2023). The minimum detectable effect sizes were f² = .075 (partial R² = .070) for children and f² = .078 (partial R² = .072) for adolescents, at 80% power and α = .05. These results suggest that the samples had reasonable sensitivity to detect effects in the small-to-moderate range, although sensitivity was more limited for smaller effects. Although these estimates do not directly establish power for quantile regression or planned contrasts between quantiles, the wide confidence intervals as shown above indicate that potentially meaningful differences across quantiles cannot be ruled out.

text.text: Over the past decade, research on reading disorders (RD) has expanded beyond its traditional focus on cognitive-linguistic factors to give increasing attention to socioemotional functioning.

The present study leveraged two existing datasets oversampled with RD (112 elementary school children aged 7 to 10 years and 110 early-and-mid adolescents aged 11 to 15 years) to examine various manifestations of reading anxiety (RA), including cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance, as well as the overall RA effects.

Our findings revealed that (1) RA was prevalent among both children and adolescents, although correlations among RA domains were stronger in adolescents than in children, (2) higher RA was moderately associated with poorer word reading performance in both age groups, (3) no significant differences in RA were observed between girls and boys, and (4) RA was negatively associated with reading performance across levels of word reading ability, with no significant evidence that the association was stronger among lower-performing readers than among middle or higherperforming readers.

These findings reinforce the observed moderate negative association between RA and reading performance in prior research and suggest that RA may affect individuals across reading levels and developmental periods.

Reading disorder (RD), also known as developmental dyslexia, is a specific learning disability characterized by persistent difficulties with accurate and/or fluent word recognition, decoding, and spelling abilities (Lyon et al., 2003), affecting approximately 5-20% of the population (Wagner et la., 2020).

The present study was motivated by two broad considerations and goals.
First, we sought to expand our understanding of different RA manifestations that are theoretically aligned with the existing anxiety and reading literature.
We leveraged secondary data that included survey items broadly covering three domains of RA manifestations: cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance.
These items capture which situations may evoke RA, and ways in which RA may manifest cognitively, physiologically, and behaviorally.

This broad categorization of RA manifestations is not intended to establish these domains as psychometrically distinct constructs, but rather provides a theoretically informed framework for examining the nature of RA.
We specifically examined RA manifestations in primary school children and early-and-mid adolescents who were enrolled in two respective studies designed to oversample participants with RD.

We then examined how each of the three domains of RA manifestations, as well as overall RA (i.e., a composite score across the three domains), was associated with word reading performance in these two cohorts.
We expected that each domain and overall RA would be negatively related to word reading performance in both samples.
Second, research on RA is still emerging, and much work remains to be done to understand the nature of the association between reading performance and RA.

In the present study, we specifically examined age-cohort and gender related differences in RA and whether the magnitude of the RA-reading association varied across the distribution of reading performance.
Existing evidence does not indicate consistent age-related differences in RA (Johnson et al., 2026).

text.text: Our understanding of age-related differences is also limited because existing research has largely focused on samples of children and adolescents either in separate studies or as a single combined group.

It is possible that RA may be higher among primary school children than among adolescents, as younger children may find reading tasks more effortful and frustrating because they are still acquiring foundational reading skills.
Additionally, primary school children are often asked to read aloud when learning to read, which may contribute to higher levels of social RA.

On the other hand, increasing reading demands in adolescence, including the emphasis on more complex tasks such as reading comprehension, as well as the accumulation of negative reading experiences over time, may contribute to higher RA among adolescents than among primary school children.
Further, we expected that the effect of age cohorts on RA would be moderated by word reading performance, with stronger age-related differences related to poorer word reading performance.
Findings on gender differences in the RA literature are also limited and mixed.

For example, Katzir et al. (2018) reported higher RA in girls than in boys, whereas Ramirez et al. (2019) did not observe overall gender differences in RA, though the negative impact of early RA on later reading development appeared to be stronger in boys than in girls.

We further examined whether potential age-cohort and gender differences in RA varied as a function of word reading performance.
Lastly, we explored whether the association between RA and word reading performance varied across the distribution of word reading performance, with particular attention to lowerperforming readers.

We chose to explore the RA-reading association across the spectrum of reading ability, motivated by evidence that RD is characterized as the lower tail of a continuous distribution of reading skill, varying in severity, rather than a discrete category between typical and impaired readers (Peterson & Pennington, 2012).

text.text: The lower portion of the reading distribution in the present study was of particular interest because both the children and adolescent datasets oversampled readers with RD or low reading achievement, allowing us to evaluate whether RA is especially relevant among readers with RD.
Meta-analytic evidence has not yet supported learning disability status as a moderator for the RA-reading association (Johnson et al., 2026).

text.text: To our knowledge, no previous study has examined whether the magnitudes of the RA-reading association vary across the reading performance distribution in both children and adolescents.

Individuals with RD are at higher risk for anxiety and other internalizing symptoms and often report lower self-esteem and face repeated academic failure and stigmatization related to reading difficulties (Chung et al., 2024; Haft et al., 2016; Katzir et al., 2018; Zuppardo et al., 2021).

text.text: Accordingly, we expected the magnitude of RA-reading association to be greater among lower performing readers, including those with RD, than among middle and higher performing readers in both cohorts.

Below is a summary of the four major research questions: (1) How frequently are the specified domains of RA manifestations, i.e., cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance, reported in the child and adolescent samples, and how are these domains and the overall RA associated with word reading performance in each sample?
(2) Does overall RA differ between the child and adolescent samples, and are age-cohort differences in RA moderated by word reading performance?
(3) Does overall RA differ by gender within the child and adolescent samples, and are gender differences in RA moderated by word reading performance within each sample?

(4) How does the magnitude of the association between overall RA and word reading performance vary across conditional quantiles of word reading performance, particularly at the lower quantiles (representing lower reading performance, including readers with RD) compared to the middle and upper quantiles (representing average and higher reading performance, respectively)?

This study drew on two datasets collected from separate reading research projects focused on different age ranges: primary school children aged 7-10 years and early-to-mid adolescents aged 11 to 15 years old.

Participants were included in the current study if they completed the RA questionnaire and correctly responded to an embedded attention-check item (i.e., "Please select 'sometimes' for this question."), ensuring data quality and adherence to task instructions.

Because the datasets sampled different age ranges, we refer to them for ease of reference as the children dataset (N = 112 [43 girls; 69 boys]; Mean age = 8.81 years, SD = .69) and the adolescent dataset (N = 110 [67 girls; 43 boys]; Mean age = 12.93 years, SD = 1.18).
Both participants' birthdates and gender were parent-reported.
The children dataset included inperson administration of the reading and RA measures, whereas all assessments in the adolescent dataset were conducted virtually.
In the children dataset, the questionnaire was completed using a pen-and-paper format, and the experimenter read each questionnaire item aloud and participants circled their responses.

In the adolescent dataset, reading measures were administered live via Webex virtually, whereas the RA questionnaire was completed independently in REDCap with a read-aloud (text-to-speech) function available.

text.text: RA was assessed using a questionnaire developed by our research team to measure anxiety experienced in reading-related situations.
Specifically, the questionnaire was designed to capture which situations may evoke RA, and ways in which RA may manifest.

Initial items were generated based on open-ended questions of RA experiences provided by 7 college mentors knowledgeable about dyslexia and were then iteratively refined through qualitative feedback and pilot testing.

During pilot testing, 80 participants responded to an initial pool of RA items and were subsequently asked to report experiences that they felt were not adequately captured by the initial item pool through open-ended questions about situations or experiences that elicited RA, associated with physiological and emotional reactions, and the effects of RA on their behaviors.
Based on the pilot testing results, items were removed, revised, or added based on patterns of exploratory analyses and the qualitive feedback from the open responses.
This iterative process resulted in a final set of 18 RA items.
The questionnaire is listed in Appendix A. The questionnaire comprised 18 RA items and 1 attention-check item (19 total).
text.formatted: The questionnaire is listed in Appendix A. The questionnaire comprised 18 RA items and 1 attention-check item <ref type="bibr">(19 total)</ref>.

text.text: Participants rated each statement on a 4-point scale from 1 (Never) to 4 (Almost Always).
During development, items were conceptually categorized into three domains, including cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance.
The domain of cognitive symptoms focuses on unpleasant thoughts and emotions related to reading, such as worry and fear.
The domain of physiological symptoms includes physiological discomfort associated with reading activities, such as stomachache and headache.
Lastly, the behavioral avoidance domain captures thoughts and behaviors related to avoidance of reading.

To ensure that the items in the questionnaire adequately represented each domain quantitatively, we conducted item screening by combining the two datasets and using separate one-factor analyses for each domain.
Within each domain, we retained items with factor loadings > .40.
text.formatted: Within each domain, we retained items with factor loadings > .40.

text.text: This resulted in 5 items in cognitive symptoms (factor loadings: .57 -.76), 4 items in physiological symptoms (factor loadings: .59 -.69), and lastly 5 items in behavioral avoidance (factor loadings: .41 -.72).
These items are bolded in the questionnaire listed in Appendix A.

Each domain had acceptable internal item consistencies for both datasets (Cognitive symptoms: Cronbach's α = .72; ωₜ = .80 in children; Cronbach's α = .86; ωₜ = .88 in adolescents; Physiological symptoms: Cronbach's α = .71; ωₜ = .76 in children; Cronbach's α = .77; ωₜ = .80 in adolescents; Behavioral avoidance: Cronbach's α = .70; ωₜ = .83 in children; Cronbach's α = .78; ωₜ = .83 in adolescents).
In behavioral avoidance, 1 item "I choose to read when given a choice" is a reverse-scored item as it reflects the opposite of behavioral avoidance in reading.
Scores were computed by summing retained items within each domain.
We also computed an overall RA composite for each participant by summing all the scores of the 3 domains.
Upon closer examination of the excluded items, we speculated possible explanations for their relatively low factor loadings.

First, the two positively worded items, "I am happy when I have to read" (cognitive domain) and "When I read, I feel relaxed" (physiological domain), may not necessarily capture the direct opposite of anxiety-related symptoms.
These items may instead reflect positive reading-related experiences that are not simply the absence of anxiety.
Their positive wording, in contrast to the other negatively worded items, may also have potentially contributed to weaker associations with the remaining items.

Second, the item "Reading things with small font and no pictures gives me a headache" may capture reading-related visual strain or effort rather than physiological symptoms specifically associated with RA.

Finally, the item "I pretend to be sick so I don't have to do reading homework" may reflect a relatively extreme form of behavioral avoidance that is less commonly experienced than other avoidance behaviors captured by the survey, such as attempting to escape reading situations or disengaging when encountering difficult words.

Because the items included in our analyses have not been psychometrically validated, we conducted an exploratory comparison with existing RA questionnaires to ensure the content of our items was broadly aligned with how RA has been operationalized in existing literature.

The results revealed that the included items in our analyses show conceptual overlap and similar content coverage to those in the Reading Anxiety Scale of Children (Grills et al., 2026) and the Reading Anxiety Test for children and Adolescents (Jones et al., 2025), two RA instruments that were formally validated.

Word-reading performance was assessed with the Test of Word Reading Efficiency-2 (TOWRE-2; Torgesen et al., 2012), using the Sight Word Efficiency (SWE; Form A) and Phonemic Decoding Efficiency (PDE; Form A) subtests.

text.text: For each timed task, participants read aloud as many words (SWE) or pseudowords (PDE) as possible, as quickly and accurately as they could, within 45 seconds.
Raw scores for each subtest were derived from the total number of items read correctly, which were then converted to age-normed standard scores.
A composite word-reading fluency score was derived from the normed TOWRE-2 Index Score based on the standard scores of the two subtests.
Reported test-retest reliability from Grades 1-12 is high, with average coefficients ranging from .89 to .93 across subtests and the index score (Torgesen et al., 2012).

To characterize response patterns across the three RA domains, we generated bar charts for each questionnaire item, showing the percentage of participants selecting each response option (i.e., Never, Sometimes, Often, and Always), relative to the total number of participants who selected that option.
These visualizations supported item-level inspection and helped to identify symptoms and behaviors that are representative of RA in each domain.

text.text: Although reading scores in the current datasets were age-normalized, they showed small associations with age in both groups, with poorer reading associated with older age in children (r = -.20, p = .04) but better reading associated with older age in adolescents (r = .20, p = .04).
In addition, the RA questionnaire scores did not have age-normed metrics.
Therefore, age was included as a control variable in the correlation analyses.

Similar to typical response patterns observed in anxiety questionnaires, each domain's RA scores and overall RA scores in the present study were found to be positively skewed, with skewness values ranging from .63 to 1.06 in children and from .82 to .98 in adolescents.

Therefore, log-transformed RA variables were used in the correlation and subsequent analyses, resulting in much reduced skewness (ranging from .01 to .28 in children and from .13 to .35 in adolescents).
Holm-Bonferroni adjustments were applied to all p-values in the correlation matrix to control for multiple comparisons.

The remaining research questions focused on overall RA effects, rather than the distinct contributions of specific RA domain; therefore, subsequent analyses used overall RA rather than the individual domain's RA scores.

To examine whether the overall RA differed between children and adolescents, and whether this difference is moderated by reading performance, we fit a linear model using the lm function in R. The model included age cohorts (children vs. adolescents), word reading performance (mean-centered), and their interaction as predictors, with the RA composite as the outcome variable.
We analyzed the interaction effects and main effects of the group.

Partial eta squared (η²partial) effect sizes were computed for the predictors of interest using Type III sums-of-squares ANOVA from the car package (Version 3.1-3, Fox & Weisberg, 2019) and the effectsize package (Version 0.8.3, Ben-Shachar et al., 2020).

text.text: Unlike traditional linear regression using ordinary least squares (OLS) to estimate the conditional mean of the outcome, QR uses a weight matrix, with observations weighted differently depending on whether they fall above or below the fitted conditional quantile, to estimate different conditional quantiles (τ) of the outcome along the distribution (Petscher & Logan, 2014).

text.text: One advantage of this approach is that it uses the full sample to estimate the RA-reading associations at specified conditional quantiles of the reading performance without requiring arbitrary cutoffs to categorize participants into discrete reading groups.

We specifically examined the association at the 25th, 50th (median), and 75th conditional quantiles of reading performance, representing relatively lower, middle, and higher levels of word reading performance, respectively.
Koenker-Bassett (KB) omnibus test was conducted to evaluate whether the overall regression coefficients varied across quantiles.
Additionally, planned pairwise contrasts were specified a priori, comparing the 25th-quantile slope with the 50th-and 75th-quantile slopes.
We used bootstrap 5000 resampling to estimate quantile-specific effects and planned contrasts between quantiles.

Word reading performance was modeled as the outcome with the overall RA composite and age as the predictors, examining whether the association between RA and reading performance varied across the distributions of reading performance after accounting for age.

text.text: Extending the existing RA research, the present study examined the multiple manifestations (i.e., cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance) of RA, as well as overall RA, and their associations with reading performance among elementary-school children and early-and-mid adolescents.

Overall, the results support 4 key preliminary findings: (1) cognitive, physiological, and behavioral avoidance manifestations of RA were frequently reported among both children and adolescents, although correlations among RA manifestations were stronger in adolescents than in children; (2) both groups showed similar magnitudes of association, with higher RA associated with poorer reading performance; (3) no significant differences in RA were observed between girls and boys; and (4) RA was negatively associated with reading performance across levels of word reading ability, with no significant evidence that the association was stronger among lower-performing readers than among middle or higherperforming readers.
These findings are discussed in the following sections, along with the study's limitations and directions for future research.
Most RA research has treated RA as a global construct.
However, recent validation work has demonstrated that RA consists of several distinct factors, including general RA, social RA, and physiological symptoms (Jones et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, recent validation work has demonstrated that RA consists of several distinct factors, including general RA, social RA, and physiological symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jones et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present study extends prior work by examining three theoretically informed manifestations of RA that have been commonly identified in the broader anxiety literature and among individuals with specific learning disabilities, including cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance (e.g., Ashcraft, 2002; Barnes et al., 2024; Eysenck & Derakshan, 2011; Willcutt & Pennington, 2000).

text.text: Descriptive statistics demonstrate that a noticeable proportion of children and adolescents report symptoms "often" and "always" related to these manifestations, with average rates across domains ranging from 21% to 27% in children and from 24% to 26% in adolescents.
These rates suggest that anxiety related to reading activities are relatively common in both elementary school and early-and-mid adolescents.
Nearly one-third of participants in both groups reported "Often" and "Always" experiencing cognitive symptoms such as worry, nervousness, and fear.
These patterns are consistent with cognitive models of anxiety that emphasize worry or fear as a central component.

About 21% of children and 25% of adolescents reported 'Often' or 'Always' experiencing physiological discomfort, which is consistent with evidence that anxiety frequently involves physiological arousal such as increased heart rate, muscle tension, and gastrointestinal discomfort (Campo, 2012; Ginsburg et al., 2006; Hale et al., 2018; Haug et al., 2004; Weems et al., 2005).

text.text: In behavioral avoidance, about 25% of both children and adolescents responded 'Often' or 'Always', with most behavioral manifestations reported similarly across groups, except for the item involving acting silly to avoid reading.
This pattern may reflect plausible developmental differences in how anxiety-related avoidance is expressed across age groups.
Alternatively, the observed difference may reflect broader age-related increases in behavioral regulation rather than specific developmental differences in anxiety expression.
Our findings indicated no significant differences in overall RA between children and adolescents.

However, the observed correlations among the three domains were numerically larger in adolescents than in children, particularly for the associations of the physiological domain with cognitive and behavioral avoidance domains.
The follow-up analyses also showed that adolescents had significantly stronger physiological-cognitive and physiological-avoidance correlations than children.
These patterns suggest that physiological responses may become increasingly interconnected with cognitive and behavioral responses to reading-related activities during adolescence.

Alternatively, it is possible that adolescents may have greater awareness of their emotional states (McRae et al., 2012), potentially leading to more consistent reporting across cognitive, physiological, and behavioral domains.
text.formatted: Alternatively, it is possible that adolescents may have greater awareness of their emotional states <ref type="bibr">(McRae et al., 2012)</ref>, potentially leading to more consistent reporting across cognitive, physiological, and behavioral domains.

text.text: In contrast, children may have more difficulty differentiating or accurately reporting these experiences, which could attenuate observed associations.
However, existing understanding of how these RA manifestations interact across development remains limited.
Future research using longitudinal designs is needed to clarify how these manifestations develop over time.
Such work would help determine when and why cognitive, physiological, and behavioral components of RA diverge or converge across development.

It is important to highlight that our current approach to categorizing the three domains of RA manifestations, although theoretically informed and aligned with the existing literature, remains preliminary.
We conducted exploratory analyses for each domain to examine whether the included items showed acceptable factor loadings and internal consistency.

To further evaluate the content of our items, we conducted a detailed item-level comparison with existing RA questionnaires, including two formally validated instruments (Grills et al., 2026; Jones et al., 2025; see Appendix B).

text.text: The comparison indicated that the items included in our analyses shared conceptual overlap with existing measures in terms of the symptoms assessed and the reading situations or activities that may elicit RA.
The comparison also showed that cognitive symptoms have received particular attention in existing RA questionnaires.

For example, Grills et al. (2026) and Ramirez et al. (2019) focused primarily on cognitive symptoms, whereas Jones et al. (2026) assessed both cognitive and physiological symptoms. Pollack et al. (2021), on the other hand, included items broadly covering all three domains examined in the present study.

text.text: Although existing validated questionnaires provide important tools for assessing RA, research in this area is still emerging, and further work is needed to understand how different manifestations of RA may be related to and potentially influence one another across development.
Importantly, the present study does not establish that the three domains represent psychometrically distinct constructs.

Accordingly, the findings of the present study should be interpreted as preliminary evidence regarding patterns of RA manifestations and their associations with word reading performance, rather than evidence supporting three psychometrically distinct dimensions of RA.
Although the items were organized into theoretically informed domains, the extent to which these domains reflect distinct underlying constructs remains unclear.

Nevertheless, examining these manifestations provides an initial understanding of how different reading-related anxiety responses are reported and associated with reading performance during childhood and adolescence.

Future research using validated instruments is needed to determine whether these patterns can be replicated and whether the different manifestations of RA represent distinguishable but potentially interrelated constructs.

Studies have shown that individuals with RD are at higher risk of developing internalizing problems such as anxiety (Francis et al., 2026; Hendren et al., 2018; Mammarella et al., 2016; McArthur et al., 2024; Nelson & Gregg, 2012; Paquette et al., 2025; Vieira et al., 2024).

text.text: The present study operationalized RD as the lower end of the continuum of reading ability, and the children and adolescent datasets oversampled reading difficulties, having more than 30% of participants qualified for RD.
Our analyses suggested that higher levels of RA were associated with poorer word reading performance.
In this sense, individuals with lower reading performance, including those with reading disorders (RD), may be more likely to experience elevated levels of RA.
This finding reinforces existing evidence that individuals with RD may be especially vulnerable to negative affective outcomes.

We further expected that RD individuals characterized at the lowest end of the reading performance distribution would have a stronger RA-reading association because they may be more likely to experience elevated RA as a result of persistent reading difficulties and repeated negative reading experiences.
However, our findings in the QR analyses do not support this prediction.

As shown in Tables 3 and 4, the RA regression coefficients were consistently negative and statistically significant across all three conditional quantiles of word reading performance in both the child and adolescent samples.
text.formatted: As shown in Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>, the RA regression coefficients were consistently negative and statistically significant across all three conditional quantiles of word reading performance in both the child and adolescent samples.

text.text: However, the strength of the RA-reading association did not differ significantly between the lower (25th) quantile and the median (50th) or upper (75th) quantiles in either sample.

Because both children and adolescent datasets included individuals with ADHD, one possible explanation for the absence of differences across reading levels is that individuals with ADHD who were not in the lower end of the reading distribution may nevertheless experience elevated RA levels comparable to those of lower-performing readers.
To address this potential confound, we conducted follow-up analyses controlling for both age and ADHD status.
The pattern of results remained unchanged.
Details of these analyses are reported in the supplementary material.
These findings suggest that although individuals with RD exhibit higher levels of RA, RD status does not appear to strengthen the association between RA and reading performance.

This interpretation aligns with findings from Johnson and colleagues' metaanalysis (2026), which reported that learning disability status did not moderate the association between RA and reading achievement.
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with findings from <ref type="bibr">Johnson and colleagues' metaanalysis (2026)</ref>, which reported that learning disability status did not moderate the association between RA and reading achievement.

text.text: Interestingly, Fishstrom et al. (2024) reported that RA predicted reading outcomes only amongst students in the middle and upper quantiles of reading achievement in the sample of struggling readers.
text.formatted: Interestingly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Fishstrom et al. (2024)</ref> reported that RA predicted reading outcomes only amongst students in the middle and upper quantiles of reading achievement in the sample of struggling readers.

text.text: The authors suggested that this pattern might reflect learned helplessness.

This explanation aligns with the idea that the development of RA may depend on how individuals interpret their reading experiences, which in turn shapes their reading-related selfconcept and contributes to anxiety symptoms (McArther, 2022; Ramirez et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This explanation aligns with the idea that the development of RA may depend on how individuals interpret their reading experiences, which in turn shapes their reading-related selfconcept and contributes to anxiety symptoms <ref type="bibr">(McArther, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Ramirez et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a task may elicit anxiety when individuals perceive themselves as lacking the ability to complete it (i.e., low self-concept).
It is also plausible that some resilient readers, despite experiencing reading difficulties, may be able to buffer against reading-related stress.
Accordingly, RD may not necessarily have a stronger negative association between RA and reading achievements.
Further studies are needed to clarify how resilience factors may moderate the relationship between RA and reading performance in both typical and RD readers.
Although the present findings did not provide evidence of age-or gender-related differences nor differences across different quantiles, smaller effects cannot be ruled out.
Post hoc sensitivity power analyses indicated that our samples had reasonable sensitivity to detect effects of small to moderate magnitudes or larger but limited sensitivity to smaller effects.

Furthermore, the 95% confidence intervals for the nonsignificant results included both negative and positive values, showing relatively wide range, indicating uncertainty regarding the magnitude and direction of potential differences.

Future studies with larger samples are needed to improve sensitivity to smaller effects and obtain more precise estimates of age-and genderrelated differences in RA, as well as potential variation in RA-reading associations across the distribution of reading performance.
The present study was limited to assessing reading performance using measures of word reading efficiency.
Therefore, the findings may not generalize to other reading tasks.
Struggling readers may be more affected by RA during tasks with higher cognitive demands, such as reading comprehension.
Nonetheless, the recent meta-analysis has reported similar associations between RA and reading achievement across different reading tasks (Johnson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, the recent meta-analysis has reported similar associations between RA and reading achievement across different reading tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Johnson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the word reading efficiency measures used in the present study are strongly correlated with broader reading outcomes, including reading comprehension (rs = .67-.84; Torgesen et al., 2012).

text.text: Taken together, the observed patterns in the present study may not be specific to the word reading alone, although future research is needed to confirm its generalizability.
Although theoretically grounded, the measures used to assess each RA domain in the current study have not yet been psychometrically validated.
Accordingly, present findings should be considered preliminary, providing initial evidence on how these domains relate to overall RA and reading performance.

Examining how cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance are expressed in RA may clarify how these systems interact and, in turn, identify potential anxiety-management targets during reading intervention for struggling readers.
However, to support generalizable and reproducible findings across studies, these measures require further psychometric evaluation.

It also bears noting that while we operationalized RD as a lower end of the word reading distribution, we did not confirm RD status through comprehensive neuropsychological testing or academic record review.
Specifically, in the children dataset we did not obtain information regarding IEPs or 504 plans for reading-related support at school.
These data may have helped us better characterize the extent of participants' reading severity and the reading support they received.
Despite its limitations, our approach may offer a uniform and replicable basis for identifying the RA-reading relation.

Future research should endeavor to collect more comprehensive data related to participants' reading difficulties as well as to collect reading achievement data across various reading subcomponents, which together would allow for a more thorough characterization of participants' reading profiles.
Interpretations regarding the development of RA to the broader population of children and adolescents are limited by the cross-sectional design and convenience samples.

The children and adolescent datasets were collected as part of different project administration and covered different age spans, with the adolescent cohort spanning a wider age range (11-15 years) than the child cohort (7-10 years).
text.formatted: The children and adolescent datasets were collected as part of different project administration and covered different age spans, with the adolescent cohort spanning a wider age range <ref type="bibr">(11-15 years)</ref> than the child cohort <ref type="bibr">(7-10 years)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the current findings may partly reflect project-specific differences and/or differences in age composition rather than developmental change.
Although reading performance was approximately normally distributed in both samples, the samples may not fully reflect the distribution of reading performance in the general population.
Future studies using representative samples are needed to examine the generalizability of these findings.

Nonetheless, the RA manifestations and the overall negative association between RA and reading performance observed in our study are largely consistent with findings from previous research, suggesting that this general pattern is not unique to our samples.

text.text: Children dataset was drawn from two cohorts recruited from North-Central Connecticut for in-persons studies.
The first cohort consisted of struggling readers enrolled in summer reading-intervention research programs.

Inclusion criteria for the intervention programs included performance at or below the 30th percentile on either the Phonemic Decoding Efficiency subtest of the Test of Word Reading Efficiency (TOWRE, Torgesen et al., 1999) or Word Attack subtest of the Woodcock Reading Mastery Test -III (Woodcock, 2011).
The second cohort was recruited for a one-time literacy research project and consisted primarily of typically developing readers.
In the children dataset, about 13% of participants (14 of 112) reported an RD diagnosis, including 5% (6 of 112) with comorbid ADHD; an additional 8% (9 of 112) reported an ADHD diagnosis without RD.
Adolescent participants were recruited virtually from across the United States and included both typically developing readers and individuals with specific learning disabilities.

The adolescent dataset had about 29% of participants (32 out of 110) reporting an RD diagnosis, including 18% (20 of 110) with comorbid ADHD; an additional 21% (23 of 110) reported an ADHD diagnosis without RD.
Among adolescents who reported an RD diagnosis, 28 out of 32 also reported receiving an Individualized Education Program (IEP) or 504 Plan at school for reading-related support.
Finally, the mechanisms underlying the RA-reading relationship, including the association between RA and RD, remain limited in the field.
Future work should investigate how other individual factors, such as the development of self-concept and resilience, interact with RA over different developmental windows.
